oil.summary: Crude markets endured a volatile session bookended by a sharp week-long sell-off and an intraday whipsaw. WTI settled near $76.34 (-0.34% on the day) after losing roughly 10% on the week, while Brent clawed back 0.61% to $80.34. The dominant driver has been the US-Iran framework deal that reopened the Strait of Hormuz and waived Iranian oil sanctions, flushing the geopolitical risk premium out of prices. An estimated 80 million barrels of crude are queued to exit Hormuz, amplifying supply-return fears. However, prices caught a brief bid in Asian trade after peace talks were reported postponed, injecting fresh uncertainty. RBOB gasoline bore the sharpest single-day pain at -3.06%. On the macro side, G7 nations agreed to escalate sanctions on Russian oil revenues, while India—well-stocked with two months of crude—is not rushing to re-engage Middle Eastern barrels.
drivers: US-Iran deal reopens Strait of Hormuz and waives Iranian oil sanctions, erasing the geopolitical premium and driving ~10% weekly decline in WTI
80 million barrels queued through Hormuz signal a near-term supply surge; Indian refiners sitting on two-month stocks, limiting immediate demand pull
Peace-talk postponement triggered a short-covering bounce; outcome remains binary and headline-sensitive

gas.summary: Natural gas sent mixed signals across regions. Henry Hub edged down 0.90% on the day to $3.204/MMBtu but remains up 6.66% on the month, suggesting underlying domestic support. TTF surged 4.08% to €42.175/MWh on the day despite a steep 9.83% weekly loss, possibly reflecting short-covering or near-term supply uncertainty as Hormuz tanker traffic reportedly stalled later in the session. The first post-deal LNG cargo transited the Strait and arrived in India, a symbolic but modest positive for Atlantic-basin flow normalization. On the supply side, Equinor committed more than $400 million to expand subsea development at the Troll gas field, adding longer-dated Norwegian supply. India also ordered a major strategic petroleum reserve expansion through ONGC. News flow specific to Henry Hub fundamentals is thin today.
drivers: First post-deal LNG cargo clears Hormuz and reaches India, signalling nascent normalization of Asian LNG flows
TTF daily spike (+4.08%) contrasts with steep weekly loss, pointing to short-covering as Hormuz tanker traffic stalled again late in the session
Equinor's $412 million Troll subsea investment adds future Norwegian gas supply, bearish for medium-term European prices

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs continued their quiet grind higher, adding 1.01% on the day to $76.14 and posting a solid 6.79% monthly gain—decoupling from the sharp monthly drop in TTF gas (-14.67%), which would ordinarily be EUA-negative via reduced gas-burn economics. The divergence may reflect structural compliance buying or broader carbon policy support. TTF's 4.08% single-day spike does, however, provide some near-term upward co-movement incentive for power-sector emitters. The Hormuz traffic stall reported late in the day—tanker movement dwindling as shippers pulled back amid renewed uncertainty—could keep short-term gas supply tighter than the deal initially implied, supporting power prices. The headline noting electricity as the binding bottleneck for AI growth underscores sustained long-run demand. Direct power-price data is not provided today, limiting further precision.
drivers: EUAs up 1.01% on the day and +6.79% on the month, defying the broader gas price slide—structural compliance demand appears to be the key support
TTF's 4.08% intraday spike and renewed Hormuz tanker traffic stall reintroduce near-term gas supply risk, offering short-run upward pressure on power generation costs
AI-driven electricity demand growth cited as a structural long-term load driver, reinforcing bullish sentiment on baseload power and carbon allowances
